prompt: A file contains `if (n > 0) {`, with parentheses. What happens to it?
hint: Run it, then run `gofmt -d` on it.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: Go has no parentheses in an `if`
choices.why: It compiled and printed `7 is positive`. Go does not need them, which is not the same as refusing them.

choices.text: It compiles and runs as written, and `gofmt` removes the parentheses
choices.why: Right. The program ran, and `gofmt -d` showed `if (n > 0) {` becoming `if n > 0 {`.

choices.text: It compiles, but `go vet` reports the parentheses as a likely mistake
choices.why: Layout is `gofmt`'s business, not `go vet`'s; `vet` looks for code that is valid and wrong.

choices.text: It compiles, and the parentheses make the condition a value of a different type
choices.why: Parentheses group an expression and change nothing about its type; `(n > 0)` is still a `bool`.

prompt: Why is an `else` that starts a line of its own, under the `if` block's closing brace, refused?
hint: What does the scanner add at the end of a line that ends in `}`?

choices.text: The compiler enforces `gofmt`'s layout, and that layout keeps `else` beside the brace
choices.why: The compiler accepts plenty `gofmt` would change, such as `if (n > 0)`. This one is grammar.

choices.text: A semicolon is inserted after the `}`, so the `if` statement has ended before `else` arrives
choices.why: Right. A line ending in `}` gets a semicolon, and no statement can begin with `else`.

choices.text: Go has no `else` after a block of more than one line
choices.why: The length of the block plays no part; `~/cond` has `} else {` after blocks of any size.

choices.text: `else` must be followed by `if`
choices.why: A plain `else {` ends the chain in `~/cond`; the trouble is where it starts, not what follows it.

prompt: `if n > 0 fmt.Println(n, "is positive")`, on one line with no braces. What does `go build` say?
hint: In Go, are the braces part of the `if`?

choices.text: Nothing: a single statement needs no braces
choices.why: That is C's rule. Go has no form of `if` without braces.

choices.text: It builds, with a warning that braces are recommended
choices.why: Go has no warnings that let a build through.

choices.text: `syntax error: unexpected name fmt, expected {`
choices.why: Right. The parser wanted the opening brace where `fmt` starts.

choices.text: `non-boolean condition in if statement`
choices.why: That is lesson 8's message for a condition that is not a `bool`; `n > 0` is one.

prompt: At the end of a line whose last token could end a statement, such as `}`, the scanner inserts a `___`.
hint: A character, or its name.

prompt: In `~/cond`, `n` is 0. Which conditions of `if n < 0 … else if n == 0 … else` are evaluated?
hint: The first true condition ends the chain.

choices.text: Only `n == 0`, because it is the one that matches
choices.why: Go cannot know which one matches without testing from the top, so `n < 0` is tested first.

choices.text: `n < 0`, then `n == 0`, and nothing after that, since it was true
choices.why: Right. `n == 0` was true, its block ran, and the chain ended.

choices.text: All of them, and then the first true one is run
choices.why: The chain stops at the first true condition; the final `else` never came into it.

choices.text: `n < 0`, and then the `else`, since `else if` is only tested after an `else`
choices.why: The chain is tested top to bottom, and `else if n == 0` comes straight after the first block.

prompt: `if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err != nil { … } else { … }`. Where can `n` be used?
hint: The `else` in `~/cond-init` printed `n`.

choices.text: Only in the first block, the one the initialiser is written on
choices.why: That is half the picture: the `else if` tested `n > 10` and the `else` printed `n`.

choices.text: Anywhere in the function after the `if`
choices.why: A line after the chain got `undefined: n`.

choices.text: In the condition and every block of the chain, and nowhere after
choices.why: Right. The names of an initialiser belong to the whole `if` statement, `else` included.

choices.text: In the `else` blocks only, because the first block runs when there was an error
choices.why: Whether a value is useful there is a different question; the first block may use `n` too.

prompt: After the chain in `~/cond-init`, still inside the loop, a line says `fmt.Println("done with", n)`. What happens?
hint: Is that line inside the `if` statement?

choices.text: It prints the last `n`, or 0 for `"forty-two"`
choices.why: That would need `n` to outlive the `if`, and it does not.

choices.text: The build fails with `undefined: n`
choices.why: Right. `n` ended with the chain's last closing brace.

choices.text: It compiles, and `go vet` reports that `n` may be unset
choices.why: It never compiles: outside the chain there is no `n` at all.

choices.text: The build fails with `declared and not used: n`
choices.why: `n` is used inside the chain; the failure is the use outside it.

prompt: Which of these are true of `if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err != nil`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about order and scope, two are beliefs.

choices.text: `strconv.Atoi(s)` runs before `err != nil` is tested
choices.why: Yes: the short statement runs first, then the condition.

choices.text: An initialiser may only hold a call that returns an `error`
choices.why: Any short statement fits; `switch ext := strings.ToLower(…); ext` used one with no error in it.

choices.text: If an `err` already exists outside, this `err` is a new variable that hides it
choices.why: Yes. The `:=` declares new names in the `if`'s block, as lesson 6 showed for a loop body.

choices.text: `n` keeps its value after the `if`, until the next initialiser replaces it
choices.why: There is no `n` after the `if`: `undefined: n`.

prompt: A function parses a number with `strconv.Atoi` and needs it in ten more lines after checking the error. Which shape fits?
hint: Where must `n` be declared to outlive the check?

choices.text: `if n, err := …; err != nil { return … }`, then use `n` below
choices.why: `n` would end with the `if`, and every use below would be `undefined: n`.

choices.text: The initialiser form, with the ten lines moved into its `else`
choices.why: It compiles, and it is the staircase the section argued against: the main path one level in.

choices.text: `n, err := …` on its own line, then `if err != nil { return … }`, and then the rest
choices.why: Right. That is `double` in `~/cond-after`: `n` is declared before the `if` and outlives it.

choices.text: The initialiser form, then `n := n` after the `if` to keep it
choices.why: After the `if` there is no `n` to copy; the right-hand `n` is just as undefined.

prompt: Put the checks of `priceFlat` in the order the function makes them.
hint: The special cases first, the ordinary price last.

prompt: In `~/cond-switch`, `"sat"` printed `weekend` and nothing else, though the `"fri"` case comes right after. Why?
hint: What ends a case in Go?

choices.text: The `"sat", "sun"` case ends with an invisible `break` that `gofmt` adds
choices.why: `gofmt` adds nothing of the kind; the rule is in the language itself.

choices.text: A case in Go ends by itself, so nothing below it ran
choices.why: Right. Go runs the first matching case and leaves the `switch`; running on would take `fallthrough`.

choices.text: `"fri"` was tested and did not match `"sat"`
choices.why: Once a case matches no further case is tested; and in C even a non-matching case below would run.

choices.text: `fmt.Println` ends the case, since it is the last call in it
choices.why: The call has no say; a case of five statements ends the same way after the fifth.

prompt: In the first `~/cond-grade`, `grade(95)` returned `pass`. Why?
hint: Read the cases from the top.

choices.text: A tagless switch tests every case and returns the last one that holds
choices.why: It is the other end: the first case that holds wins, and the rest are not tested.

choices.text: `>=` compares the scores as text, and `"95"` sorts before `"90"`
choices.why: `score` is an `int`; the comparison is numeric and `95 >= 90` is true.

choices.text: The compiler rejected the overlapping case and dropped it
choices.why: Nothing was rejected; the compiler does not compare conditions with each other.

choices.text: `score >= 50` held and came first, so `score >= 90` was never tested
choices.why: Right. Putting the narrowest condition first gave `95 distinction`.

prompt: In `~/cond-fall`, `n := 5` becomes `n := 200`. How many lines does the program print?
hint: `fallthrough` moves one case down, once.

prompt: A `switch` with nothing after the keyword compares each case with `___`.
hint: A predeclared boolean.

prompt: Match each file name to what `~/cond-ext` printed after it.
hint: `filepath.Ext`, then `strings.ToLower`.

prompt: A case ends with `fallthrough`, and the next case's condition is false. What happens?
hint: `~/cond-fall` printed that 5 is more than 100.

choices.text: The next case is skipped, and the program tries the one after it
choices.why: That would mean `fallthrough` tests conditions, and it does not test any.

choices.text: The program goes to `default`
choices.why: `default` did not run in `~/cond-fall`; the body under `n > 100` did.

choices.text: The `switch` ends there, as if `fallthrough` were `break`
choices.why: Then `5 is more than 100` would not have been printed.

choices.text: The next case's body runs anyway
choices.why: Right. `fallthrough` transfers control to the next body without evaluating its condition.

prompt: A C programmer writes `case "sat":` with nothing under it, then `case "sun": fmt.Println(d, "weekend")`. What does Go print for `"sat"`?
hint: An empty case is still a whole case.

choices.text: `sat weekend`, because an empty case runs on into the next one
choices.why: That is C. In Go the empty `"sat"` case matches, runs nothing, and ends.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right. The `"sat"` case matched and had no statements; `case "sat", "sun":` is the Go spelling.

choices.text: A compile error, because a case may not be empty
choices.why: An empty case is legal Go; it compiles and does nothing when it matches.

choices.text: A compile error, `duplicate case`, because both cases print the same line
choices.why: `duplicate case` is about the same value in two cases; `"sat"` and `"sun"` differ.

prompt: Which of these compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are refusals you saw captured.

choices.text: A `switch` whose `default` is written first, above the cases
choices.why: Yes. `default` runs only when no case matched, wherever it is written.

choices.text: A `fallthrough` as the last statement of the last case
choices.why: Refused: `cannot fallthrough final case in switch`.

choices.text: A tagless `switch` whose cases overlap, such as `score >= 50` above `score >= 90`
choices.why: Yes, and that is the trouble: it compiled and graded 95 as a pass.

choices.text: Two cases of one `switch d` that both list `"sat"`
choices.why: Refused: `duplicate case "sat" … in expression switch`.

prompt: `if x := f(); x > 3 { … } else if y := g(); y > x { … } else { … }`. Which names can the final `else` use?
hint: Each initialiser's names last to the end of the chain, from where they are declared.

choices.text: Neither: each initialiser's names belong to its own block
choices.why: The `else` in `~/cond-init` printed `n`, so an initialiser's names reach past its own block.

choices.text: Only `x`, the first initialiser's
choices.why: The `else if` has an initialiser of its own, and its `y` reaches the `else` below it too.

choices.text: Both `x` and `y`
choices.why: Right. `x` lasts from the first initialiser to the end of the chain, and `y` from the second.

choices.text: Only `y`, the nearest initialiser's
choices.why: `y > x` in the `else if` already used `x`, and it lasts to the end of the chain.

prompt: `func main()` on one line and `{` alone on the next. What does the compiler say, and why?
hint: The same mechanism refuses `else` on its own line.

choices.text: `unexpected semicolon or newline before {`: the line ending in `)` got a semicolon
choices.why: Right. `)` can end a statement, so a semicolon was inserted after it, and the brace came too late.

choices.text: Nothing: it compiles, and `gofmt` moves the brace up
choices.why: It does not compile, and `gofmt` cannot read the file either: it stops with the same message.

choices.text: `missing function body`: Go reads `func main()` alone as a declaration
choices.why: The captured message was about the semicolon before `{`, not a missing body.

choices.text: `syntax error: unexpected {`: Go has no blocks that stand alone
choices.why: Go does have blocks that stand alone; the message named the inserted semicolon.
